transcript:
Operator
Greetings, welcome to the DMC Global's Q3 Earnings Call. At this time, all participants are in listen only mode. A question-and-answer session will follow the formal presentation. If anyone should require operator assistance during the conference, please press star zero on your telephone keypad. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. It is now my pleasure to introduce your host, Geoff High, VP of Investor Relations. Thank you, Geoff. You may begin.
Geoff High
VP of Investor Relations, DMC Global
Hello, and welcome to DMC's Q3 Conference Call. Presenting today are President and CEO, Jim O'Leary, and Chief Financial Officer, Eric Walter. I'd like to remind everyone that matters discussed during this call may include forward-looking statements that are based on our estimates, projections, and assumptions as of today's date and are subject to risks and uncertainties that are disclosed in our filings with the SEC. Our business is subject to certain risks that could cause actual results to differ materially from those anticipated in our forward-looking statements. DMC assumes no obligation to update forward-looking statements that become untrue because of subsequent events. Today's earnings release and a related presentation on our Q3 performance are available on the investors page of our website located at dmcglobal.com.
A webcast replay of today's presentation will be available at our website shortly after the conclusion of this call. With that, I'll now turn the call over to Jim O'Leary. Jim?
Jim O'Leary
President and CEO, DMC Global
Thank you, Geoff, and thank you to everyone joining us for today's call. While challenging market conditions continued to impact each of DMC's businesses during Q3, we made significant progress on the most important strategic objective within our control, the continued deleveraging of our balance sheet. By the end of Q3, our net debt had been reduced to $30.1 million, down 47% since the start of the year and the lowest level since we purchased the controlling interest in Arcadia at the end of 2021. DMC's consolidated Q3 sales were $151.5 million, down 1% versus Q3 a year ago, while Adjusted EBITDA attributable to DMC was $8.6 million, up 51% year-over-year.
At Arcadia, our building products business, Q3 sales totaled $61.7 million, a 7% year-over-year increase, but down 1% from Q2. Adjusted EBITDA attributable to DMC more than doubled to $5.1 million from the year ago quarter, reflecting improved operating performance and better absorption of fixed manufacturing overhead due to the sales increase. Adjusted EBITDA was up 27% sequentially. The efforts to stabilize Arcadia's business during the past year have helped mitigate the impact of stubbornly high interest rates and generally soft commercial construction activity in Arcadia's core western region, where architectural billings have declined every month since May, according to the Architecture Billings Index. At DynaEnergetics, our energy products business, Q3 sales were $68.9 million, down 1% year-over-year and up 3% sequentially.
The Q3 was marked by declining activity in DynaEnergetics' core US onshore market, where well completions were down 8% year-over-year and 6% sequentially. At the end of the quarter, active frac crews, a key indicator of demand, were down nearly 20% from the 2025 peak in March. DynaEnergetics reported Q3 Adjusted EBITDA of $4.9 million, up from break even in the year ago quarter, down 46% sequentially. The sequential decline reflects lower product pricing and higher costs due to tariffs, as well as certain receivable and inventory charges. At NobelClad, our composite metal business, Q3 sales were $20.9 million, down 16% year-over-year, down 21% sequentially.
The declines reflect the delayed impact of lower US bookings during Q1 and Q2 when customers moved to the sidelines as they monitored fluctuating US and reciprocal tariff policies. Adjusted EBITDA was $2.1 million, down 64% from the prior year and 53% sequentially, reflecting lower absorption of fixed manufacturing overhead on reduced sales and a less favorable product mix. During Q3, NobelClad booked a $20 million order associated with a large international petrochemical project. After quarter end, we received an additional $5 million order related to that same project. Together, these bookings, which ship at the beginning of next year, reflect the largest order in the 60-year history of NobelClad. NobelClad's backlog at the end of Q3 was $57 million, up 53% from Q2, not including the $5 million follow-on.
I'll now turn the call over to Eric for a closer look at our Q3 results and our outlook for the Q4.
Eric Walter
CFO, DMC Global
Thank you, Jim. I'll start off with a closer look at Q3 profitability. As Jim mentioned, consolidated Adjusted EBITDA attributable to DMC was $8.6 million. Inclusive of the Arcadia non-controlling interest, Adjusted EBITDA was $12 million or 7.9% of sales, up from 4.6% in Q3 last year and down from 10.4% in Q2. The year-over-year increase in EBITDA margin principally reflects improved results at DynaEnergetics, which was impacted by $5 million in inventory and bad debt charges in last year's Q3, as well as price-driven top-line growth at Arcadia, leading to improved absorption of fixed manufacturing overhead. The sequential decline in Adjusted EBITDA margin was primarily due to lower pricing and higher costs at DynaEnergetics, as well as reduced activity levels at NobelClad.
Arcadia's Q3 Adjusted EBITDA margin before non-controlling interest allocation improved to 13.8% from 5.8% in the year-ago quarter, and 10.9% in the Q2. Dyno's Adjusted EBITDA margin improved to 7.1% in the Q3 compared to less than 1% in last year's Q3. EBITDA margin was down from 13.4% in the Q2 for the reasons previously mentioned. NobelClad's Q3 Adjusted EBITDA margin was approximately 10% and was impacted by the tariff-related booking slowdown earlier in the year. Adjusted EBITDA margin was down from 23.2% in the Q3 last year and 16.5% in the Q2.
Q3 SG&A expense was $26 million, or 17.1% of sales, versus $28.2 million or 18.5% of sales in Q3 last year. Q3 adjusted net loss attributable to DMC was $1.6 million, while adjusted loss per share attributable to DMC was $0.08. With respect to liquidity, we ended Q3 with cash and cash equivalents of approximately $26.4 million. Total debt was $56.5 million, down 20% from the end of 2024. As Jim mentioned, net debt was $30.1 million, down 47% from the end of last year. Now on to guidance. We expect Q4 sales to be in a range of $140 to 150 million.
While Adjusted EBITDA attributable to DMC is expected in a range of $5 to 8 million. Our guidance reflects the lag of converting recent record bookings at NobelClad into sales, which are expected in 2026. Our guidance range also anticipates continued headwinds in DynaEnergetics' core North American market, which has been significantly impacted by both tariffs and declining well completion activity, and may experience a seasonal slowdown late in the quarter, as has been the case in recent years. Although Arcadia is expected to experience a normal seasonal Q4 slowdown, it expects continued year-over-year improvement in profitability due to better operational execution. Our guidance is heavily influenced by macroeconomic concerns, volatility, and visibility issues created by the current state of energy markets and tariff policies and is subject to change either upward or downward as market conditions evolve.
With that, I'll turn it back to Jim for some additional comments.
Jim O'Leary
President and CEO, DMC Global
Thanks, Eric. In an environment marked by volatile and declining energy prices, elevated interest rates, and shifting tariff policies, we continue to focus on what's in our control. DynaEnergetics is containing its costs while pursuing international opportunities and navigating an extremely challenging North American oil and gas market. As discussed and based on direct customer feedback, we expect the oilfield services market to face continued headwinds during Q4. Accordingly, we remain focused on the self-help measures within our control. As mentioned earlier, NobelClad secured a record order that its commercial team worked nearly five years to win while it rebuilds its order book and looks globally for new business opportunities. Finally, at Arcadia, we've stabilized operations after a challenging 2024 and are positioning the business for an eventual recovery in its commercial and residential markets.
Arcadia has now had several quarters of stability since we brought Jim Sladen back, and we believe we've successfully reset the business while we wait for market conditions to improve. Collectively, we've made substantial progress on our most important initiative, deleveraging our business. This remains our principal corporate objective as we work through generally challenging markets for each one of our operating companies. Our progress would not be possible without the hard work of our DMC associates, and I wanna thank them for their continued contributions. With that, we're ready to take any questions. Operator?
Operator
Thank you. We will now be conducting a question-and-answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star one on your telephone keypad. A confirmation tone will indicate your line is in the question queue. You may press star two if you would like to remove your question from the queue. For participants using speaker equipment, it may be necessary to pick up your handset before pressing the star keys. One moment, please, while we poll for questions. Thank you. Our first question comes from the line of Gerry Sweeney with Roth Capital Partners. Please proceed.
Gerry Sweeney
Senior Research Analyst, ROTH Capital Partners
Good afternoon, Jim, Eric, Jeff. Thanks for taking my call.
Jim O'Leary
President and CEO, DMC Global
Hey, Gerry.
Eric Walter
CFO, DMC Global
Hey, Gerry. You're welcome.
Gerry Sweeney
Senior Research Analyst, ROTH Capital Partners
Start off with Arcadia. Jim, I know you mentioned, the ABI was down, I think, out in the West, etc. Two questions on that front. One, are you seeing any green shoots? Two, are there opportunities for additional operational improvements at Arcadia, or is that level set for now?
Jim O'Leary
President and CEO, DMC Global
Oh, okay. We're seeing green shoots, but remember, that's very specific to us. What we had when I think the industry was still doing okay, and I would say just okay, both residential and commercial. You know, with turnover and some self-inflicted issues, we had a challenging two or three years after the acquisition. A lot of our year-over-year improvement, our month-over-month improvement, a lot of the things we're seeing are just introducing stability with Jim back, bringing back some employees who might have, you know, looked for greener pastures, repairing some of the relationships that might have gotten a bit frayed, both on the supplier side, on the customer side. We're seeing some Arcadia-specific green shoots, but I wouldn't read too much into that.
Gerry Sweeney
Senior Research Analyst, ROTH Capital Partners
Okay.
Jim O'Leary
President and CEO, DMC Global
From everything you can see, it's observable and anecdotal, whether it's our public peers, even one like JELD-WEN today, which is, you know, far more residential than us. You know, it's a data point. If you subscribe to any of the credit agencies, you can see companies like Oldcastle and Conair. You know, we're all struggling with exactly the same issues. Persistently high interest rates, you know, overall cost and affordability, and that applies to commercial as well. You know, I think that should start getting better, but I wouldn't say you see the green shoots industry-wide. A board of a company I'm on, I mean, we're in every MSA in the country.
If you put a gun to my head, I couldn't tell you what MSA in the country is really doing well. Maybe one or two in the Carolinas. All of our, you know, year-over-year improvement and, you know, green shoots that you categorize, all very Arcadia specific, and all because we brought back stability and some self-help measures. On what we can do specifically, stabilize things, brought back some key players, repaired relationships, really soft, you know, the soft skills, which Jim is fantastic at. You know, Jim would have a longer list of things that we can do next than I would.
A lot of it is, you know, we can still do better in terms of professionalization, maybe bringing some new skills in, maybe looking at, you know, we've been underspending CapEx for a while on things that, you know, we're gonna have some decisions to make as to where and when we wanna put it in. You know, this capital we might have put in in 2021 that we have to do. Whether or not you do it now, if you think you're still gonna be bouncing along the bottom, is a really important question. You know, we both have very long lists of things we can do that would be. I would say it's past self-help.
It would be, okay, you know, now we're at the point where professionalization, bringing some new skills, you know, we're getting there now on the ERP implementation, some of the improvement, the data quality for the first time, you know, in a while. There's a long list of things we work on, including on capacitization. The question is when, you know, when's the right time? You don't want to add it early if the market just doesn't, you know, doesn't fill up a paint line or fill up an anodizing line, right?
Gerry Sweeney
Senior Research Analyst, ROTH Capital Partners
Yes. Understood. Yeah. Got it. Switching gears, NobelClad, large order. It sounded like it was gonna ship in, my words, Q1, but I'm not sure how you exactly characterized it. You know, what would be the cadence of the shipping of that order and over how many quarters, if more than one, would this sort of take place?
Jim O'Leary
President and CEO, DMC Global
Yeah. I said 2026, but look, Eric will give you the particulars. It's more back-end loaded than Q1.
Gerry Sweeney
Senior Research Analyst, ROTH Capital Partners
Okay.
Eric Walter
CFO, DMC Global
Yeah. I don't.
Jim O'Leary
President and CEO, DMC Global
No, no. I understood. Okay, fine.
Eric Walter
CFO, DMC Global
Yeah. No, I don't have much to add to that other than, like Jim said, it'll be second half of 2026 is where you're gonna see the bulk of the revenue from that order.
Gerry Sweeney
Senior Research Analyst, ROTH Capital Partners
Got it. Just sticking with NobelClad, obviously, that's a large international order. US is facing some headwinds. You know, I think there's a lot of opportunity in the Gulf at some point for some of this petrochemical stuff, but I'm just curious if you're seeing any additional orders unlock, or are they still tied up because of tariffs and other issues and just uncertainties?
Jim O'Leary
President and CEO, DMC Global
Well, we agree, and we hope you're right about further petrochemical orders. Right now, if you asked the division president there how he'd categorize, you know, the state of things, and we've, you know, went through his budget a couple of times in the last few months. You know, if you have the choice of order or wait, people wait, you know? It's.
Gerry Sweeney
Senior Research Analyst, ROTH Capital Partners
Got it.
Jim O'Leary
President and CEO, DMC Global
You know, the tariffs were a big issue that impacted us early, particularly on one or two really big ones that we know, we probably didn't get because of tariffs. Right now, I think it's just a general level of economic uncertainty. You know, outside of tech and a couple of really fair-haired favored sectors, if you're very capital intensive, if you're very consumer driven, if you're very, and consumer meaning the ultimate end markets, you can include automotives in there. You know, I mean, nobody's rushing to do capital projects unless you're bringing stuff back under some of the Trump policies, you know, factory building, major CapEx. You're gonna wait before you order until you start to be a little bit more comfortable with the overall economy.
Gerry Sweeney
Senior Research Analyst, ROTH Capital Partners
Got it. Okay. I'll jump back in queue. Thanks.
Jim O'Leary
President and CEO, DMC Global
Great. Thank you, Gerry.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Katie Fleischer with KeyBanc Capital Markets. Please proceed.
Katie Fleischer
Analyst, KeyBanc Capital Markets
Hey, good evening, guys. I wanted to dig into the tariff impacts in Dyna a little bit. How should we think about that impact in coming quarters, and is there any opportunity to push price within that market?
Eric Walter
CFO, DMC Global
Yeah. The impact to Dyna in the quarter was roughly $3 million. To answer your question, to try to push price in the market, that's extremely challenging right now. All of the players in the market are pretty much going through the same type of issues with importing steel and some other components that are used in their perforating systems. What we're doing right now is trying to figure out ways we can be more efficient with how we manufacture our products and being smart about the automation that we put into our manufacturing line. To increase price is very difficult in the market right now.
Katie Fleischer
Analyst, KeyBanc Capital Markets
Yep. Makes sense. Just any other details that you could give around the margin progression within Dyna and NobelClad for next quarter? Like, does the midpoint of guidance assume that both of those are going to see a sequential decline?
Eric Walter
CFO, DMC Global
Well, I think for just taking them one at a time, with Dyna, they're gonna continue to have the pressures that we talked about from a pricing standpoint. There may be some seasonal slowdown. To the extent that there is, that puts additional pressure on margins because there's less sales and less volume to absorb their fixed manufacturing overhead. The same would be true of NobelClad. The large order that we talked about, will ship in 2026, so we're probably not gonna get much of a benefit, you know, for the next bit, few quarters. Same thing, it's gonna be to the extent that the sales are a little soft in the quarter, it's gonna put pressure on them because they're not gonna be able to absorb that overhead.
You know, you can take that into, you know, your modeling and it should show you that the margins will be pressured, you know, quarter-over-quarter.
Katie Fleischer
Analyst, KeyBanc Capital Markets
Yep.
Jim O'Leary
President and CEO, DMC Global
The only thing I'd add to that, I would add, you know, if your assumption, whatever your assumptions are on end markets will probably be right ahead. You know, whether it's lead by a couple of months, lead by a quarter, it'll be right ahead of our margin progression because everything at NobelClad for the most part has been absorption driven. A fair amount, outside of the tariffs, which Eric just went through, there's a little bit of mix, but it's the pricing issue and the fact that the Permian is so challenging right now. You know, when you think both of those end markets get better, you'll see our margins pick up, you know, maybe disproportionately.
I'd like to think we have some operating leverage, but it'll be very end market, dependent because I think we, you know, did the self-help things early. You still, you know, and NobelClad's the best example. You know, you're down $5 million of sales, that's all throughput, and that all comes through as overhead absorption.
Katie Fleischer
Analyst, KeyBanc Capital Markets
Got it. Just one last question here. I know visibility is very limited, but just looking ahead, when you think about the recovery of these end markets, how much more downside is there from here? What would you really need to see to give you some confidence that some of these demand trends are starting to pick up?
Jim O'Leary
President and CEO, DMC Global
Well, look, I mean, the first thing you need is stability. I am encouraged, and I would think the stability in the order book at NobelClad is a precursor. You know, we won't see that for a quarter or two or, you know, two or more as it's mostly back-end, back-end weighted. The fact that the order book picked up, we got a, you know, a major biggest in our history order is a real positive. In the building industry, I think we have more self-help and more benefits just from being stable. It, it's still a really, really tough market. The fact that the Fed has started cutting interest rates, you know, some appropriate consternation as to whether or not the next move will be up or flat, you know, after Powell's last couple of comments.
You know, you got a Fed that seems more favorably disposed, particularly with the recent appointees. You know, it's not clear that you're gonna see three or four cuts the way people might have been thinking a month or two ago, or that'll be dragged out over a longer period. You know, that is absolutely critical to get things going. I'd like to think we could see some green shoots sooner, but I still think you got a grand total of 20 permits issued in some of the parts of Southern California that we're most, you know, most long-term excited for, but there's just not a lot of activity. You know, they're continuing to keep a lid on permits.
The activity is not there the way, you know, honestly, the way some of these poor homeowners would like to see. You know, when that starts to loosen up, that'll be a little bit divorced from interest rates. Building, you know, if we get two or three cuts, building could start picking up in the back half of next year. I would say if you listen to home builder calls, some of the larger distributors like Builders FirstSource, Beacon, you know anybody that's out there, I wouldn't say they've written off next year, but they're very, very conservative about it because we've been burned a few too many times.
That's, you know, I think middle end of next year would be optimistic on housing, but I think we have, you know, we have some specific things that are Arcadia and Arcadia dependent. You know, honestly, the market I'm least knowledgeable about is obviously Dyna, just from past history. You know, that's the one where the volumes have held up, but it's a couple of industry prognosticators out there. You know, they do comment on how consolidated our customers and our customers' customers have gotten. We're still at the point where, you know, we've probably had the brunt of the tariffs that we've had to eat.
Once, you know, once the markets take off and we get the opportunity to, you know, be selling the value that we bring, you know, I think we'll get some of the margin and price back, but that's probably quarters away. You know, if you wake up and the Saudis decide they're not gonna keep the spigots open, that could change tomorrow.
Katie Fleischer
Analyst, KeyBanc Capital Markets
All right, fair enough. Thanks for all the color.
Jim O'Leary
President and CEO, DMC Global
You're welcome. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Stephen Gengaro with Stifel. Please proceed.
Stephen Gengaro
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, Stifel
Hi. Thanks for the question. I guess just based on what we've been hearing around a lot of these US pressure pumping companies, it seems like activity levels are kind of bottoming, and that's kind of the direction that we're heading. I guess more specifically, can you talk about or elaborate expectations for 2026, specifically within the perforating gun business and maybe also what current pricing looks like in that business? I just have a quick follow-up. Thanks.
Jim O'Leary
President and CEO, DMC Global
Too early to talk about 2026. We're, you know, we're one quarter at a time for good reason. The visibility is terrible. We don't comment on pricing other than if the market picks up and it's a little less competitive, we should see some relief. We're nowhere near there right now.
Stephen Gengaro
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, Stifel
Got it. I guess just more specifically for oriented perforating guns, we've kinda heard that it's been having a positive impact on production levels. I guess, could you maybe talk about what you're seeing in the field?
Jim O'Leary
President and CEO, DMC Global
That's true. We have a product. Yeah, we have a product out there. It's a self-orientating gun as well. Yeah. Technology is what's driven a lot of the incredible production increase, increases in the Permian for in the last 10 years. We've been a leader there and continue to be.
Stephen Gengaro
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, Stifel
Got it. Thank you.
Jim O'Leary
President and CEO, DMC Global
You're welcome.
Operator
Thank you. There are no further questions at this time. I'd like to pass the call back over to James O'Leary for any closing remarks.
Jim O'Leary
President and CEO, DMC Global
Look, we appreciate your patience. We are doing everything we can under the category of self-help and positioning ourselves for the eventual recovery. We didn't get a chance to talk about it except in the prepared remarks, you know, getting the balance sheet in shape, having your cost structure in shape, being ready for whether it's opportunities or just the things we gotta deal with next year and having a clean balance sheet, plenty of cash flow and a cost structure that'll accommodate us are the things we're working on. We appreciate your patience, and for any employees listening, we appreciate your hard work and dedication. Thank you.
Operator
This concludes today's teleconference. You may disconnect your lines at this time. Thank you for your participation.
